h.strategy: Read the retrieved abstracts for measured results that contradict common heuristics: options that were expected to be weak but did well, gains that vanished in strong configurations, or components whose value depended on what else was present. Turn each such finding into a conditional claim about when a one-field edit's effect is larger or smaller. Each hypothesis must cite the kind of evidence it rests on in one sentence. Avoid hypotheses that only restate that removing an alternative path makes the remaining path matter more. Vary the edited and conditioning fields, and balance HIGHER and LOWER.

hyps.why: Benchmark-wide accuracy results show diminishing returns from extra conv3x3 edges, so the gain is smaller when the parallel direct edge already has conv3x3.

Edge 0's output reaches the output through fewer conv paths when edge 2 is removed, so upgrading it should help less, a pattern consistent with path-dependent component value in NAS-Bench-201 analyses.
Replacing a dead final edge with a conv3x3 recovers a large amount of accuracy, much more than replacing an existing parametric op, as seen in the heavy penalty for 'none' in known results.
Replacing a conv3x3 with a skip on the direct edge typically costs accuracy, whereas replacing weaker ops (pool or none) with skip often helps.
Pooling was expected to be a harmless cheap substitute but is consistently weaker than convs, so swapping a conv3x3 for it hurts more than swapping other ops.
A direct skip complements a deep conv-heavy path by easing optimization, so its gain should be larger when edge 5 carries conv3x3.
Skip beats pooling on the same edge because pooling blurs features, so replacing pooling with skip gains more than replacing other ops.
Removing the first edge's conv3x3 cuts the main feature extractor, so it loses more accuracy than removing a pool or skip there.
Gains from extra conv3x3 saturate when the other input to node 2 already carries a conv3x3.
Cheap conv1x1 recovers a lot over a missing edge, much more than it gains when replacing an existing op.
